items.stem: Define the term "rapport".
items.answer: A relationship of trust and mutual understanding between the anthropologist and the people studied, which makes access to everyday life possible
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a relationship of trust and mutual understanding between the anthropologist and the people studied, which makes access to everyday life possible. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why participant observation usually takes a long time.
items.answer: Rapport takes time to build, people behave less for the observer as they get used to them, seasonal and life-cycle events must be seen, and learning the language and implicit rules requires extended immersion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rapport takes time to build, people behave less for the observer as they get used to them, seasonal and life-cycle events must be seen, and learning the language and implicit rules requires extended immersion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a structured survey and participant observation.
items.answer: Participant observation involves long-term, flexible immersion that yields rich qualitative understanding of meanings in context; a structured survey asks many people the same fixed questions, giving comparable, quantifiable data but little insight into context or practice.
items.markingKey: Participant observation involves long-term, flexible immersion that yields rich qualitative understanding of meanings in context; a structured survey asks many people the same fixed questions, giving comparable, quantifiable data but little insight into context or practice. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The longer an anthropologist stays, the more objective the research becomes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Longer fieldwork deepens understanding but does not remove the researcher's positionality; involvement may also increase, so reflexivity is still required.
items.markingKey: Longer fieldwork deepens understanding but does not remove the researcher's positionality; involvement may also increase, so reflexivity is still required. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

By my third week on the fishing boat I had stopped being sick. The crew no longer laughed when I fell over; they shouted at me to coil the ropes instead. During the night shift, Rui told me the real reason they avoid the northern grounds: not the weather, as the captain says in interviews, but because "the Spanish boats take everything and the inspectors never come". I wrote this down on my phone in the toilet, where nobody could see. The next morning the captain asked what I was always typing. I said I was writing to my mother.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a fishing boat off the coast of Portugal.

Describe how the anthropologist's relationship with the crew changes in the text, as presented in the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: At first the crew laughed at the anthropologist's falls; by the third week they gave instructions (coil the ropes), treating them as a working member; Rui shared a confidential explanation during the night shift; the captain became curious about the note-taking.
items.markingKey: At first the crew laughed at the anthropologist's falls; by the third week they gave instructions (coil the ropes), treating them as a working member; Rui shared a confidential explanation during the night shift; the captain became curious about the note-taking. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Bourgois's fieldwork in East Harlem (1985–1990) shows the strengths and risks of participant observation.
items.answer: Bourgois lived in El Barrio, spent nights in crack houses, recorded conversations with dealers and witnessed violence. Immersion gave him access to dealers' own accounts of respect and humiliation, but also exposed him to danger and difficult ethical choices about what to record and publish.
items.markingKey: Context (Bourgois lived in El Barrio, spent nights in crack houses, recorded conversations with dealers and witnessed violence.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: immersion gave him access to dealers' own accounts of respect and humiliation, but also exposed him to danger and difficult ethical choices about what to record and publish. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the strengths and risks of participant observation.

With reference to social relations, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific. Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.
items.answer: Text: Sharing work built rapport, so Rui revealed information that contradicts the captain's public interview account – showing the gap between official and private explanations. But it also creates difficulties: covert note-taking, a misleading answer to the captain, and the risk of betraying Rui's confidence, raising questions of consent and honesty. Ethnography – Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918): In the kula ring, men on different islands keep lifelong partnerships through the ceremonial exchange of shell valuables: soulava necklaces travel clockwise and mwali armshells anticlockwise, creating alliances between communities rather than profit. Comparison: similarities and differences in how social relations is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Respond to the big question "Is there such a thing as a universal human experience?" by drawing on the experience of long-term fieldwork, the concept of culture and Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) or another ethnography.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies culture explicitly and uses ethnography: Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies culture explicitly and uses ethnography: Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation. items.stem: Explain why participant observation helps to reveal the difference between ideal and real behaviour.
items.answer: Interviews capture norms people state, whereas living alongside them shows what they actually do in everyday situations, including contradictions, compromises and unspoken rules.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Interviews capture norms people state, whereas living alongside them shows what they actually do in everyday situations, including contradictions, compromises and unspoken rules. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between observation and participation.
items.answer: Participation means taking part in activities to experience them from within; observation means watching and recording systematically. Ethnographers balance both, and the balance shapes the data obtained.
items.markingKey: Participation means taking part in activities to experience them from within; observation means watching and recording systematically. Ethnographers balance both, and the balance shapes the data obtained. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), explain how the key concept of culture helps us to understand the experience of long-term fieldwork.
items.answer: Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An extended account of one person's life, gathered over several interviews, used to show how wider social processes shape individual experience"?
options: netnography
multi-sited ethnography
reflexivity
life history
items.answer: life history
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of life history.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an unstructured interview and a structured interview.
items.answer: A structured interview uses a fixed set of questions in the same order for comparability; an unstructured interview is a guided conversation that follows the participant's concerns, producing richer but less comparable data.
items.markingKey: A structured interview uses a fixed set of questions in the same order for comparability; an unstructured interview is a guided conversation that follows the participant's concerns, producing richer but less comparable data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Elena writes: "Field notes are the finished ethnography." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Field notes are raw data; the ethnography is a later analytical and written product that selects, interprets and theorises from them.
items.markingKey: Field notes are raw data; the ethnography is a later analytical and written product that selects, interprets and theorises from them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I spread the family tree on the floor of the courtyard. Grandmother Sita corrected me at once: her late husband's brother's son should not be on the same line as her own sons "because they eat separately since the quarrel". She asked me to remove a woman I had included as a cousin: "She married outside; we do not count her." Her granddaughter, Priya, quietly added the woman back when Sita went inside. Later I photographed the family; Sita insisted that the sons stand at the front and the daughters-in-law behind.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a joint household in rural Nepal.

Explain, with close reference to the text, what the text reveals about the genealogical and visual methods. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: Both methods are not neutral records: the genealogy is shaped by present relationships (commensality, quarrels) and by judgements about who "counts" (exclusion after marriage outside), and different members (Sita, Priya) contest it; the photograph stages hierarchy by gender and generation. The methods reveal classification and power within the household.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both methods are not neutral records: the genealogy is shaped by present relationships (commensality, quarrels) and by judgements about who "counts" (exclusion after marriage outside), and different members (Sita, Priya) contest it; the photograph stages hierarchy by gender and generation. The methods reveal classification and power within the household. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: With reference to De León's Undocumented Migration Project, explain how it illustrates mixed methods in ethnography.
items.answer: The project combined interviews with migrants, photography, forensic science and the archaeology of discarded objects in the Sonoran Desert. Combining material, visual and interview data documented experiences that no single method could capture, especially the deaths of migrants who could not be interviewed.
items.markingKey: Context (The project combined interviews with migrants, photography, forensic science and the archaeology of discarded objects in the Sonoran Desert.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: combining material, visual and interview data documented experiences that no single method could capture, especially the deaths of migrants who could not be interviewed. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to mixed methods in ethnography.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa and Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, compare and contrast the role of culture in the collection of ethnographic data.
items.answer: Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926)): Mead argued that adolescence in Samoa was relatively free of the stress seen in the United States, supporting Boas's view that culture rather than biology shapes development; Derek Freeman's 1983 critique disputed her findings. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far culture is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "visual anthropology"?
options: Research in which participants are co-researchers who help shape questions, interpretation and writing
A person who controls or facilitates the researcher's access to a group or setting
The social position of the researcher – gender, age, ethnicity, class, nationality, religion – relative to the people studied, which affects access and interpretation
The use and study of photography, film and other images both as research methods and as objects of anthropological analysis
items.answer: The use and study of photography, film and other images both as research methods and as objects of anthropological analysis
items.markingKey: D. "visual anthropology" is the use and study of photography, film and other images both as research methods and as objects of anthropological analysis.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that interviews are less valuable than participant observation? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Interviews and observation answer different questions and are strongest together.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: people may say what they think the researcher wants; interviews capture norms rather than practice; interviews reveal meanings, memories and life histories that cannot be observed; they give participants a voice in their own terms. Suitable ethnographies include Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa, De León's The Land of Open Graves. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Interviews and observation answer different questions and are strongest together. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "the "reflexive turn""?
options: A person who controls or facilitates the researcher's access to a group or setting
The movement in the 1980s, associated with Writing Culture (Clifford and Marcus, 1986), that questioned ethnographic authority and urged attention to the author's role
Research in which participants are co-researchers who help shape questions, interpretation and writing
The practice of critically examining how the anthropologist's own background, assumptions and presence shape the research and its account
items.answer: The movement in the 1980s, associated with Writing Culture (Clifford and Marcus, 1986), that questioned ethnographic authority and urged attention to the author's role
items.markingKey: B. "the "reflexive turn"" is the movement in the 1980s, associated with Writing Culture (Clifford and Marcus, 1986), that questioned ethnographic authority and urged attention to the author's role.

items.stem: Explain the difference between reflexivity and self-indulgence.
items.answer: Reflexivity analyses how the researcher's presence shapes knowledge in order to improve the account; self-indulgence makes the researcher's feelings the main subject, displacing the people studied.
items.markingKey: Reflexivity analyses how the researcher's presence shapes knowledge in order to improve the account; self-indulgence makes the researcher's feelings the main subject, displacing the people studied. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Positionality only matters when the anthropologist is a foreigner." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Positionality also shapes insider research, through gender, class, age and family ties within one's own community (e.g. Hurston in Eatonville).
items.markingKey: Positionality also shapes insider research, through gender, class, age and family ties within one's own community (e.g. Hurston in Eatonville). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify one way in which social relations matters in Briggs's Never in Anger (with an Utku Inuit family at Chantrey Inlet in the Canadian Arctic (fieldwork 1963–1965)) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Briggs lived as an adopted daughter in an Utku household; after she spoke angrily to visiting white fishermen who wanted to borrow the Utku canoe, she was quietly ostracised for months.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Briggs lived as an adopted daughter in an Utku household; after she spoke angrily to visiting white fishermen who wanted to borrow the Utku canoe, she was quietly ostracised for months. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Jean Briggs, Never in Anger: Portrait of an Eskimo Family (1970), with an Utku Inuit family at Chantrey Inlet in the Canadian Arctic (fieldwork 1963–1965)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When I first arrived at the hostel for nursing students, the women called me "auntie" and stopped talking when I entered the kitchen. I was forty, foreign and childless, and they were nineteen. Everything changed the evening I burned the rice: they laughed until they cried and showed me how to soak it first. After that, Grace began to tell me about the senior nurses who shout at students in front of patients. "You won't write that," she said, half asking. I realised that my age, which had kept me out, now made her see me as someone who might complain on her behalf.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a nursing students' hostel in the Philippines.

With reference to the concept of identity, analyse how the anthropologist's positionality shapes the research in the text. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Age, nationality and childlessness first created distance ("auntie"); a shared, humbling domestic mistake reduced status differences and created rapport; later the same age and outsider status made Grace see the researcher as a potential advocate, so positionality shapes both access and the expectations participants place on the researcher. Reflexive notes make this visible.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Age, nationality and childlessness first created distance ("auntie"); a shared, humbling domestic mistake reduced status differences and created rapport; later the same age and outsider status made Grace see the researcher as a potential advocate, so positionality shapes both access and the expectations participants place on the researcher. Reflexive notes make this visible. items.stem: Briefly explain why being an insider is not automatically an advantage in fieldwork.
items.answer: Insiders may take practices for granted, be positioned within local factions, face pressure to represent the group positively, or be denied access because of their own gender, class or family; outsiders may be allowed to ask "naive" questions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Insiders may take practices for granted, be positioned within local factions, face pressure to represent the group positively, or be denied access because of their own gender, class or family; outsiders may be allowed to ask "naive" questions. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "collaborative ethnography"?
options: Both the method of long-term fieldwork and the written (or filmed) account that results from it
The core anthropological method of living with and taking part in the everyday life of a group over a long period while systematically observing and recording it
Research in which participants are co-researchers who help shape questions, interpretation and writing
The movement in the 1980s, associated with Writing Culture (Clifford and Marcus, 1986), that questioned ethnographic authority and urged attention to the author's role
items.answer: Research in which participants are co-researchers who help shape questions, interpretation and writing
items.markingKey: C. "collaborative ethnography" is research in which participants are co-researchers who help shape questions, interpretation and writing.

items.stem: Explain why collaborative ethnography is seen as more ethical.
items.answer: Sharing control over questions, interpretation and writing reduces the researcher's power over representation and makes the research more useful and accountable to participants.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sharing control over questions, interpretation and writing reduces the researcher's power over representation and makes the research more useful and accountable to participants. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Mariam runs a Facebook group for women from her village who now live in Doha, Milan and Leeds. Each Friday they post photographs of what they have cooked, and the women still in the village comment on whether the dough has been rolled thinly enough. When Mariam's cousin in Milan posted a cake bought from a shop, three aunts left the group in protest, then rejoined a week later. Mariam has asked me to help write a booklet of the recipes, "so the girls born abroad will have them". We decided together which recipes and which family names to include.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an online community linking a Moroccan village with its migrants.

Explain, with close reference to the text, how the text illustrates multi-sited and collaborative ethnography. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: The field is spread across a village and three cities, connected online, so the anthropologist follows relationships rather than a place; online food posts maintain belonging and moral judgement across distance; the recipe booklet is collaborative – Mariam and the anthropologist decide together what to include, sharing control over representation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The field is spread across a village and three cities, connected online, so the anthropologist follows relationships rather than a place; online food posts maintain belonging and moral judgement across distance; the recipe booklet is collaborative – Mariam and the anthropologist decide together what to include, sharing control over representation. Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Using the Why We Post project (2016) as an example, explain comparative digital ethnography.
items.answer: Nine anthropologists spent about fifteen months each in sites from Trinidad to rural China studying what people post and why. It showed that social media are shaped by local cultures, so "the same" platform is used very differently in different places.
items.markingKey: Context (Nine anthropologists spent about fifteen months each in sites from Trinidad to rural China studying what people post and why.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it showed that social media are shaped by local cultures, so "the same" platform is used very differently in different places. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparative digital ethnography.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Digital ethnography is as valid as traditional fieldwork."
items.answer: Digital ethnography is valid when it applies the same rigour and links online and offline contexts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: online life is real social life with its own norms; it reaches dispersed or hidden communities. Arguments against: researchers may miss offline contexts that shape online behaviour; consent and identity verification are difficult; platforms control access and data. Supported judgement: Digital ethnography is valid when it applies the same rigour and links online and offline contexts.

items.stem: Explain why online worlds can be legitimate field sites.
items.answer: People form real relationships, norms, economies and identities online; participant observation in those spaces reveals social life as it is lived there (Boellstorff).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: People form real relationships, norms, economies and identities online; participant observation in those spaces reveals social life as it is lived there (Boellstorff). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Mariam runs a Facebook group for women from her village who now live in Doha, Milan and Leeds. Each Friday they post photographs of what they have cooked, and the women still in the village comment on whether the dough has been rolled thinly enough. When Mariam's cousin in Milan posted a cake bought from a shop, three aunts left the group in protest, then rejoined a week later. Mariam has asked me to help write a booklet of the recipes, "so the girls born abroad will have them". We decided together which recipes and which family names to include.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an online community linking a Moroccan village with its migrants.

To what extent could the research described in the text be carried out ethically? Refer to informed consent, harm and representation. Consider the ethics of publication as well as of the fieldwork itself.
items.answer: Posts in a closed group are not public, so the consent of members (not only the administrator) is needed; photographs and family names in the booklet raise questions of anonymity versus credit; the aunts' protest is a sensitive family matter. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Posts in a closed group are not public, so the consent of members (not only the administrator) is needed; photographs and family names in the booklet raise questions of anonymity versus credit; the aunts' protest is a sensitive family matter. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. items.stem: Which of the following is the main strength of participant observation?
options: It can be completed in a single day
It reveals the gap between what people say and what they do
It produces statistically representative samples
It requires no relationship with participants
items.answer: It reveals the gap between what people say and what they do
items.markingKey: B. Long-term presence shows practice, not only stated norms.

items.stem: Who systematised the genealogical method in anthropology?
options: Marcel Mauss
Franz Boas
W. H. R. Rivers
Clifford Geertz
items.answer: W. H. R. Rivers
items.markingKey: C. Rivers developed it during the 1898 Torres Strait Expedition and published it in 1910.

items.stem: Malinowski's private fieldwork diary, published in 1967, caused controversy because it:
options: revealed his frustration with and contempt for some Trobrianders
showed he had never visited the Trobriands
contained secret kula maps
was written in Kiriwinian
items.answer: revealed his frustration with and contempt for some Trobrianders
items.markingKey: A. A Diary in the Strict Sense of the Term exposed a gap between his public ethos and private feelings.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Multi-sited ethnography is simply visiting many places briefly." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is defined by following meaningful connections (people, things, ideas) between sites, and still requires sustained engagement in each.
items.markingKey: It is defined by following meaningful connections (people, things, ideas) between sites, and still requires sustained engagement in each. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Participant observation is unscientific because the researcher is involved." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Participant observation is systematic (field notes, cross-checking, long duration) and its involvement is a strength that yields valid insider understanding; reflexivity addresses bias.
items.markingKey: Participant observation is systematic (field notes, cross-checking, long duration) and its involvement is a strength that yields valid insider understanding; reflexivity addresses bias. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why genealogies remain useful even when kinship is not the topic.
items.answer: They map who is related to whom, revealing inheritance, residence, alliances, migration and who participates in events, so they provide a framework for understanding social relations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They map who is related to whom, revealing inheritance, residence, alliances, migration and who participates in events, so they provide a framework for understanding social relations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an insider anthropologist and an outsider anthropologist.
items.answer: An insider shares membership of the community studied and may have easier access and language skills but may overlook the familiar; an outsider must learn the culture and may see the taken-for-granted more clearly but may misunderstand meanings. Most anthropologists are partly both.
items.markingKey: An insider shares membership of the community studied and may have easier access and language skills but may overlook the familiar; an outsider must learn the culture and may see the taken-for-granted more clearly but may misunderstand meanings. Most anthropologists are partly both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between multi-sited ethnography and single-sited ethnography.
items.answer: Single-sited ethnography studies one bounded location in depth; multi-sited ethnography follows connections across locations, gaining breadth but sometimes losing depth in each site.
items.markingKey: Single-sited ethnography studies one bounded location in depth; multi-sited ethnography follows connections across locations, gaining breadth but sometimes losing depth in each site. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between participant observation and a structured survey.
items.answer: Participant observation involves long-term, flexible immersion that yields rich qualitative understanding of meanings in context; a structured survey asks many people the same fixed questions, giving comparable, quantifiable data but little insight into context or practice.
items.markingKey: Participant observation involves long-term, flexible immersion that yields rich qualitative understanding of meanings in context; a structured survey asks many people the same fixed questions, giving comparable, quantifiable data but little insight into context or practice. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline how belonging shapes the collection of ethnographic data, using evidence from Basso's Wisdom Sits in Places.
items.answer: Knowing the names and stories of the land is part of belonging to the community and links people across generations.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Knowing the names and stories of the land is part of belonging to the community and links people across generations. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Keith Basso, Wisdom Sits in Places: Landscape and Language among the Western Apache (1996), among the Western Apache of Cibecue, Arizona); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to belonging. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Briefly describe Weiner's restudy of the Trobriand Islands (1970s) and explain what it reveals about gendered positionality.
items.answer: As a woman, Weiner was invited into women's mortuary exchanges that Malinowski had largely ignored. The ethnographer's gender shaped which activities were seen and valued, so Weiner's account corrected a male-centred picture of exchange.
items.markingKey: Context (As a woman, Weiner was invited into women's mortuary exchanges that Malinowski had largely ignored.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the ethnographer's gender shaped which activities were seen and valued, so Weiner's account corrected a male-centred picture of exchange. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gendered positionality.

items.stem: With reference to Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001), explain how the key concept of change helps us to understand research that follows people across places and online.
items.answer: "Social remittances" – ideas, behaviours and identities – flowed from Boston to Miraflores, changing gender roles, politics and religious practice in the village.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: "Social remittances" – ideas, behaviours and identities – flowed from Boston to Miraflores, changing gender roles, politics and religious practice in the village. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001), among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to change. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

By my third week on the fishing boat I had stopped being sick. The crew no longer laughed when I fell over; they shouted at me to coil the ropes instead. During the night shift, Rui told me the real reason they avoid the northern grounds: not the weather, as the captain says in interviews, but because "the Spanish boats take everything and the inspectors never come". I wrote this down on my phone in the toilet, where nobody could see. The next morning the captain asked what I was always typing. I said I was writing to my mother.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a fishing boat off the coast of Portugal.

With reference to the concept of social relations, analyse what the text shows about the strengths and difficulties of participant observation. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Sharing work built rapport, so Rui revealed information that contradicts the captain's public interview account – showing the gap between official and private explanations. But it also creates difficulties: covert note-taking, a misleading answer to the captain, and the risk of betraying Rui's confidence, raising questions of consent and honesty.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Sharing work built rapport, so Rui revealed information that contradicts the captain's public interview account – showing the gap between official and private explanations. But it also creates difficulties: covert note-taking, a misleading answer to the captain, and the risk of betraying Rui's confidence, raising questions of consent and honesty. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I spread the family tree on the floor of the courtyard. Grandmother Sita corrected me at once: her late husband's brother's son should not be on the same line as her own sons "because they eat separately since the quarrel". She asked me to remove a woman I had included as a cousin: "She married outside; we do not count her." Her granddaughter, Priya, quietly added the woman back when Sita went inside. Later I photographed the family; Sita insisted that the sons stand at the front and the daughters-in-law behind.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a joint household in rural Nepal.

Using evidence from the text, describe how the members of the household responded to the genealogy and the photograph. Refer to at least three specific details from the text.
items.answer: Sita corrected the placement of her husband's brother's son because the families "eat separately"; she asked for a woman who married outside to be removed; Priya added her back when Sita left; Sita arranged the photograph with sons in front and daughters-in-law behind.
items.markingKey: Sita corrected the placement of her husband's brother's son because the families "eat separately"; she asked for a woman who married outside to be removed; Priya added her back when Sita left; Sita arranged the photograph with sons in front and daughters-in-law behind. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Explain how Briggs's Never in Anger illustrates the concept of social relations. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Briggs lived as an adopted daughter in an Utku household; after she spoke angrily to visiting white fishermen who wanted to borrow the Utku canoe, she was quietly ostracised for months.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Briggs lived as an adopted daughter in an Utku household; after she spoke angrily to visiting white fishermen who wanted to borrow the Utku canoe, she was quietly ostracised for months. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Jean Briggs, Never in Anger: Portrait of an Eskimo Family (1970), with an Utku Inuit family at Chantrey Inlet in the Canadian Arctic (fieldwork 1963–1965)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: "Insider anthropologists produce better ethnography than outsiders." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Neither position is inherently better; quality depends on reflexive awareness of the position held.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: language skills and access (Hurston, Simpson); less risk of exoticising; insiders may overlook the familiar or be constrained by loyalties; outsiders can ask naive questions; the insider/outsider distinction is a continuum (Abu-Lughod's "halfie"). Suitable ethnographies include Rosaldo's "Grief and a Headhunter's Rage", Briggs's Never in Anger, Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Neither position is inherently better; quality depends on reflexive awareness of the position held. — Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an online community linking a Moroccan village with its migrants.

Compare and contrast how space, place and time is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013)). Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: The field is spread across a village and three cities, connected online, so the anthropologist follows relationships rather than a place; online food posts maintain belonging and moral judgement across distance; the recipe booklet is collaborative – Mariam and the anthropologist decide together what to include, sharing control over representation. Ethnography – Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013), with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005): Holmes crossed the US–Mexico border with Triqui companions and was detained by the Border Patrol, showing how the border distributes risk unequally between bodies. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Malinowski's phrase for the small, routine details of daily life that can only be observed by living among people"?
options: key informant
ethnography
imponderabilia of actual life
participant observation
items.answer: imponderabilia of actual life
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of imponderabilia of actual life.

items.stem: Define the term "visual anthropology".
items.answer: The use and study of photography, film and other images both as research methods and as objects of anthropological analysis
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the use and study of photography, film and other images both as research methods and as objects of anthropological analysis. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which book (1986) is most associated with the "crisis of representation" in anthropology?
items.answer: Writing Culture, edited by James Clifford and George Marcus
items.markingKey: Writing Culture, edited by James Clifford and George Marcus. Writing Culture questioned the authority of the ethnographic text.

items.stem: A student claims: "Online interactions are not 'real' and so cannot be studied ethnographically." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Online interaction produces genuine relationships, norms and identities, as Boellstorff and the Why We Post project show.
items.markingKey: Online interaction produces genuine relationships, norms and identities, as Boellstorff and the Why We Post project show. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The longer an anthropologist stays, the more objective the research becomes." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Longer fieldwork deepens understanding but does not remove the researcher's positionality; involvement may also increase, so reflexivity is still required.
items.markingKey: Longer fieldwork deepens understanding but does not remove the researcher's positionality; involvement may also increase, so reflexivity is still required. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a structured interview and an unstructured interview.
items.answer: A structured interview uses a fixed set of questions in the same order for comparability; an unstructured interview is a guided conversation that follows the participant's concerns, producing richer but less comparable data.
items.markingKey: A structured interview uses a fixed set of questions in the same order for comparability; an unstructured interview is a guided conversation that follows the participant's concerns, producing richer but less comparable data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Positionality only matters when the anthropologist is a foreigner." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Positionality also shapes insider research, through gender, class, age and family ties within one's own community (e.g. Hurston in Eatonville).
items.markingKey: Positionality also shapes insider research, through gender, class, age and family ties within one's own community (e.g. Hurston in Eatonville). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Online interactions are not 'real' and so cannot be studied ethnographically." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Online interaction produces genuine relationships, norms and identities, as Boellstorff and the Why We Post project show.
items.markingKey: Online interaction produces genuine relationships, norms and identities, as Boellstorff and the Why We Post project show. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between participation and observation.
items.answer: Participation means taking part in activities to experience them from within; observation means watching and recording systematically. Ethnographers balance both, and the balance shapes the data obtained.
items.markingKey: Participation means taking part in activities to experience them from within; observation means watching and recording systematically. Ethnographers balance both, and the balance shapes the data obtained. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A photograph is an objective record that needs no interpretation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Photographs are framed, selected and interpreted; they reflect the photographer's choices and power, and their meanings depend on context and audience.
items.markingKey: Photographs are framed, selected and interpreted; they reflect the photographer's choices and power, and their meanings depend on context and audience. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When I first arrived at the hostel for nursing students, the women called me "auntie" and stopped talking when I entered the kitchen. I was forty, foreign and childless, and they were nineteen. Everything changed the evening I burned the rice: they laughed until they cried and showed me how to soak it first. After that, Grace began to tell me about the senior nurses who shout at students in front of patients. "You won't write that," she said, half asking. I realised that my age, which had kept me out, now made her see me as someone who might complain on her behalf.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a nursing students' hostel in the Philippines.

Using evidence from the text, describe how the students' treatment of the anthropologist changes. Write in your own words and keep close to the evidence in the extract.
items.answer: At first they called the anthropologist "auntie" and stopped talking in the kitchen; after the rice was burned they laughed and taught the anthropologist; Grace then shared criticisms of senior nurses; she asked, half-questioning, whether it would be written.
items.markingKey: At first they called the anthropologist "auntie" and stopped talking in the kitchen; after the rice was burned they laughed and taught the anthropologist; Grace then shared criticisms of senior nurses; she asked, half-questioning, whether it would be written. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Explain how the Why We Post project illustrates the concept of social relations. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Social media mostly extend existing relationships – such as ties with migrant kin – rather than creating entirely new ones.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Social media mostly extend existing relationships – such as ties with migrant kin – rather than creating entirely new ones. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Daniel Miller and colleagues, How the World Changed Social Media (Why We Post project, 2016), in a comparative digital ethnography by nine anthropologists in nine field sites, including Brazil, Chile, England, India, Italy, Trinidad, Turkey and two sites in China); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to social relations. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

By my third week on the fishing boat I had stopped being sick. The crew no longer laughed when I fell over; they shouted at me to coil the ropes instead. During the night shift, Rui told me the real reason they avoid the northern grounds: not the weather, as the captain says in interviews, but because "the Spanish boats take everything and the inspectors never come". I wrote this down on my phone in the toilet, where nobody could see. The next morning the captain asked what I was always typing. I said I was writing to my mother.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a fishing boat off the coast of Portugal.

Identify and describe how the anthropologist's relationship with the crew changes in the text. Refer closely to the text. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: At first the crew laughed at the anthropologist's falls; by the third week they gave instructions (coil the ropes), treating them as a working member; Rui shared a confidential explanation during the night shift; the captain became curious about the note-taking.
items.markingKey: At first the crew laughed at the anthropologist's falls; by the third week they gave instructions (coil the ropes), treating them as a working member; Rui shared a confidential explanation during the night shift; the captain became curious about the note-taking. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

I spread the family tree on the floor of the courtyard. Grandmother Sita corrected me at once: her late husband's brother's son should not be on the same line as her own sons "because they eat separately since the quarrel". She asked me to remove a woman I had included as a cousin: "She married outside; we do not count her." Her granddaughter, Priya, quietly added the woman back when Sita went inside. Later I photographed the family; Sita insisted that the sons stand at the front and the daughters-in-law behind.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a joint household in rural Nepal.

With reference to the concept of classification, analyse what the text reveals about the genealogical and visual methods. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: Both methods are not neutral records: the genealogy is shaped by present relationships (commensality, quarrels) and by judgements about who "counts" (exclusion after marriage outside), and different members (Sita, Priya) contest it; the photograph stages hierarchy by gender and generation. The methods reveal classification and power within the household.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Both methods are not neutral records: the genealogy is shaped by present relationships (commensality, quarrels) and by judgements about who "counts" (exclusion after marriage outside), and different members (Sita, Priya) contest it; the photograph stages hierarchy by gender and generation. The methods reveal classification and power within the household. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Weiner's restudy of the Trobriand Islands (1970s) shows gendered positionality.
items.answer: As a woman, Weiner was invited into women's mortuary exchanges that Malinowski had largely ignored. The ethnographer's gender shaped which activities were seen and valued, so Weiner's account corrected a male-centred picture of exchange.
items.markingKey: Context (As a woman, Weiner was invited into women's mortuary exchanges that Malinowski had largely ignored.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the ethnographer's gender shaped which activities were seen and valued, so Weiner's account corrected a male-centred picture of exchange. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gendered positionality.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Holmes's research following Triqui migrants shows multi-sited ethnography.
items.answer: Holmes worked with Triqui families in Oaxaca, crossed the border with them, and followed them to farms in Washington and California. Following people across sites revealed connections between village poverty, border policy and farm labour hierarchies that no single site could show.
items.markingKey: Context (Holmes worked with Triqui families in Oaxaca, crossed the border with them, and followed them to farms in Washington and California.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: following people across sites revealed connections between village poverty, border policy and farm labour hierarchies that no single site could show. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to multi-sited ethnography.

items.stem: Using Geertz's "Deep Play" and Bourgois's In Search of Respect, compare the ways in which power is experienced and contested by the people studied.
items.answer: Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)): In "deep" matches between high-status men the money matters less than the status symbolically at stake, so the cockfight dramatises the village status hierarchy without actually changing it. Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)): Bourgois links street violence and drug dealing to structural forces: the loss of factory jobs, racism, and the humiliation dealers felt in service-sector office jobs. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account. Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: "Interviews are less valuable than participant observation." Discuss.
items.answer: Interviews and observation answer different questions and are strongest together.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: people may say what they think the researcher wants; interviews capture norms rather than practice. Arguments against: interviews reveal meanings, memories and life histories that cannot be observed; they give participants a voice in their own terms. Supported judgement: Interviews and observation answer different questions and are strongest together. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When I first arrived at the hostel for nursing students, the women called me "auntie" and stopped talking when I entered the kitchen. I was forty, foreign and childless, and they were nineteen. Everything changed the evening I burned the rice: they laughed until they cried and showed me how to soak it first. After that, Grace began to tell me about the senior nurses who shout at students in front of patients. "You won't write that," she said, half asking. I realised that my age, which had kept me out, now made her see me as someone who might complain on her behalf.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a nursing students' hostel in the Philippines.

With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. You may refer to ethical codes, but apply them to the situation described.
items.answer: Grace's criticism of senior nurses could put her training at risk; her question signals uncertain consent, so the anthropologist must clarify what will be published, anonymise the hostel and avoid raising expectations of advocacy that cannot be met. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Grace's criticism of senior nurses could put her training at risk; her question signals uncertain consent, so the anthropologist must clarify what will be published, anonymise the hostel and avoid raising expectations of advocacy that cannot be met. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. Markbands – 9–10: insightful, balanced discussion of ethical dilemmas, competing obligations and possible responses, fully grounded in the text and professional codes; 7–8: well-developed discussion of several ethical issues and competing obligations, closely linked to the text; 5–6: relevant ethical issues explained with reference to the text and to professional principles; 3–4: some relevant ethical issues (e.g. consent, harm) identified and partly explained with reference to the text; 1–2: ethical issues identified only in general terms, with little reference to the text; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: "Why do people hold on to tradition in times of rapid change?" With reference to the Why We Post project and the key concept of change, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies change explicitly and uses ethnography: Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies change explicitly and uses ethnography: Rather than social media changing people everywhere in the same way, people changed social media to fit local norms – the "attainment" of each site's values. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion. Markbands – 9–10: perceptive, well-argued response integrating key concepts, ethnography and theory, with a reasoned conclusion; 7–8: clear argument that applies the key concept to ethnographic material and considers more than one perspective; 5–6: relevant response using a key concept and an ethnography, with some analysis; 3–4: some relevant ideas; ethnographic or conceptual support is thin or general; 1–2: limited response to the big question; assertions with little anthropological support; 0: does not reach the standard described below.
